blocks.text: **The problem.** Given a string `s`, return how many of its substrings are palindromes. Substrings at different positions count separately, even if they contain the same letters.

Below, the even middle in the gap between the two b's grows to bb and then to abba. In all, abba has six palindromic substrings: a, b, b, a, bb and abba.

blocks.text: The pattern: expand around the centre

A palindrome is a mirror image around its **middle**. If you know `s[i..j]` is a palindrome, then `s[i-1..j+1]` is one exactly when the two new end letters are equal. So instead of testing each substring separately, start from a middle and **grow outwards** one step at a time, counting every step that still matches — and stop at the first mismatch, because nothing wider with that middle can be a palindrome.

Odd-length palindromes have a **letter** in the middle (`"aba"`), even-length ones have a **gap** (`"abba"`). A string of n letters has n letters and n - 1 gaps: **2n - 1 middles**. Growing from all of them finds every palindromic substring, in O(n²) time and O(1) space.
**Time O(n³), space O(1).** About n² / 2 substrings, each checked in up to O(n). Checking `"abba"` repeats the work of checking `"bb"`.

blocks.caption: From each of the 2n - 1 middles, every step outwards that still matches is one more palindrome.

blocks.code:
def count_substrings(s):
    count = 0

    def expand(left, right):              # grow outwards while the ends match
        nonlocal count
        while left >= 0 and right < len(s) and s[left] == s[right]:
            count += 1                    # s[left..right] is a palindrome
            left -= 1
            right += 1

    for center in range(len(s)):
        expand(center, center)            # odd length: one middle letter
        expand(center, center + 1)        # even length: the gap after it
    return count

blocks.text: **Time O(n²), space O(1).** 2n - 1 middles, and each grows at most n / 2 steps. A string of identical letters is the worst case: every step matches.

blocks.alt: Test every substring: O(n³) time, O(1) space. Expand each centre: O(n²) time, O(1) space.

blocks.text: A dynamic-programming table (`pal[i][j]` is true when the ends match and `pal[i+1][j-1]` is true) also counts them in O(n²) time, but needs O(n²) memory. Expanding gets the same speed for free. Manacher's algorithm does it in O(n), but it's rarely expected in interviews.

items: **All the same letter** — n(n + 1) / 2, the maximum: `"aaaa"` has 10.
**No letter repeats** — just the n single letters.
**Forgetting even centres** — `"aa"` would give 2 instead of 3.
**Longest Palindromic Substring** — the same expansion, remembering the widest one. Next lesson.
**Palindrome Partitioning** — split a string into palindromes in every possible way: backtracking, with these checks (or a precomputed table) to prune.
**Longest Palindromic Subsequence** — letters may be skipped: that's a different problem, solved with dynamic programming (Pattern 9's style).
